name: Language Models and Diagnosis
blurb: How medical language models compare with physicians.
title: Language Models and Diagnosis
answer: Medical language models now pass licensing exam style questions comfortably; Med-PaLM 2 scored about 86.5 percent on the MedQA dataset. Exam scores are not clinical performance, and studies of real diagnostic reasoning show mixed results that depend heavily on how clinicians use the tool.

reading.body:
Med-PaLM 2 scored about 86.5 percent on MedQA licensing exam questions, but exam scores are not clinical performance.

The pattern is a gap between benchmark accuracy and diagnostic reasoning in practice. A model can clear a licensing-style question set and still produce mixed results when it is used on real cases. The data attributes that variance to how clinicians use the tool, which places the human in the loop as a variable rather than a constant.

For AI specifically, this matters because the compute behind a medical language model buys question-answering ability, not judgment. The scarce input is not the model's knowledge but the workflow around it. The stated position is that diagnostic AI should function as a second opinion that must justify itself, not as an answer key.

What this does not cover is the size of any clinical effect, the number of studies behind the mixed results, or which conditions and settings were tested. It gives one benchmark figure and one deployment principle, and nothing about cost, latency, or the infrastructure that would serve such a model at a hospital.

sections.body: Treat diagnostic AI as a second opinion that must justify itself, not as an answer key.
